utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I suppose, Mr. Black, you are still busy cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, in fact, Your Honour, I had just finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You had just finished. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic? I beg your pardon, Mr. Perovic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, following the cross-examination my learned friend from the Prosecution completed yesterday, I would like to ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to do this to you. I forgot to remind the witness that he is still bound by the declaration that he took at the beginning of his testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Some of the questions in the cross-examination had to do with units of the Territorial Defence, and I would like to ask you a couple of questions in connection with that. First, according to the law and the constitution of the SFRY, did the federal units of the former SFRY have their own armed forces? Did they have that, according to the law on defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were republic armies or armed forces, in fact, those Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And finally, what were the units of Territorial Defence? Under the law and defence and the constitution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the Territorial Defence were the second of two components of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The first component was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of the questions asked of you in cross-examination were related to the army's goals. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that regard, what, under the SFRY constitution, was the main obligation of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main constitutional obligation of the Yugoslav army was to protect the territorial integrity of the country and its constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the critical period, that is from 1990 to 1992, who was Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Federal Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that man, in his capacity of Federal Secretary for National Defence, was the number one in the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is he indicted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but I just note that that last question was a leading question, and on redirect, I believe he needs to ask questions in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure I understand how, in what way my question is leading. I asked the witness if he knew who Veljko Kadijevic was in that period and if he's aware of any proceedings against that man before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question asked about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I didn't think that question asked about proceedings before this Tribunal, Mr. Perovic. If I may read the question to you, you said: "Do you know that that man, in his capacity of Federal Secretary for National Defence, was the number one in the armed forces of the SFRY?" Now, so as to ask the question in a non-leading fashion, you should say: As Federal Secretary of the National Defence force, what is his position in the SFRY, in the armed forces of the SFRY? Then you will get an answer from him. You don't tell him the answer. Do you now see how it was leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, and I accept that, but I think there was maybe a confusion due to a misinterpretation, perhaps. I asked the witness if he knew who Veljko Kadijevic was, in the period from 1990 to 1992 and the witness said that, yes, he knew he was Federal Secretary for National Defence, that is man number one in the armed forces of the SFRY. And my second related question was whether he was aware of any proceedings before that man before this Tribunal. And that was my question. But maybe that did not feature in the record and maybe that caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see it on the record. Maybe that is the cause of the confusion. Mr. Black, are you able to come to our rescue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I can think of -- perhaps because there's a slight delay in the translation in English, I objected -- before I heard the question about was he indicted by the Tribunal, I was objecting to the preceding question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that may be the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And maybe the question about the Tribunal then never got interpreted because then there was an objection. Okay. But that is the question that was being objected to, Mr. Perovic. Not the one about the Tribunal. But now if it is the one preceding the question about the Tribunal, do you accept or do you dispute that it was leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I understand, Your Honour, but my question was not leading. I repeat: I asked the witness if he was aware who, in 1990 to 1992, Veljko Kadijevic was, and he answered me that he knew that the man was Federal Secretary for National Defence. And then I asked my next question. Maybe the Prosecutor didn't hear it. The question was if the witness was aware of any proceedings before this Tribunal against that man, in view of the fact that he used to be Federal Secretary for National Defence, and those were my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's probably clear this point with you. You never asked the witness if he knew that Veljko Kadijevic, in his capacity as Federal Secretary for National Defence, was the number one in the armed forces of the SFRY? You never asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was: Was he aware who, in the critical period from 1990 to 1992, Veljko Kadijevic was, in which position he was. And the witness answered me that he was Federal Secretary for National Defence. That was my first question. And the second related question was whether he was aware of any proceedings before this Tribunal against that person. Those were my questions. Maybe the interpretation was not precise enough. Maybe that's the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, I'm reading what is written here, and that is why I was asking you if you didn't ask this question that is written here. And if you didn't ask that question, I just want you to say to me, No, I never asked that question. Then if you never asked that question, the objection falls also. Now, I know you asked him whether he knew who he was and he said, yes, he was the Federal Secretary of the armed forces. Your next question was: "Thank you. Some of the questions asked of you in cross-examination were related to the army's goals. Do you remember that?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Now, in that regard, what, under the SFRY constitution, was the main obligation of the Yugoslav army." Then he explained that. Wait a minute. I beg your pardon. "Thank you. In the critical period, that is from 1990 to 1992, who was Veljko Kadijevic?" "He was Federal Secretary for National Defence." "Do you know that that man, in his capacity of Federal Secretary for National Defence, was the number one in the armed forces of the SFRY?" I'm just asking you: You never asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Well, that question, then, will be expunged from the record because it was never asked, and I think, if so, your objection will follow it. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The next question regarding the position of Veljko Kadijevic is: Are you aware, Mr. Peric, of any proceedings before this Tribunal against that man?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, from media reports, that there are proceedings against him in Croatia, but I don't know about this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some questions were asked of you in cross-examination related to blockades imposed on the military installations of the Yugoslav People's Army, and the Prosecutor asked you whether those military installations, from the standpoint of Croatian armed forces, could have been considered as legitimate military targets, legitimate in the eyes of the Croatian armed forces, of course. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that regard, in 1991, in the summer and autumn of 1991 - that's the period we're discussing - in the territory of what is now the former Yugoslavia, what was the only recognised international entity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as an internationally recognised entity still existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that territory, was there another internationally recognised entity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from that country, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the territory of the former Yugoslavia in the same period, what was the only regular armed force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only regular armed force were the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the JNA and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Some questions related to your involvement in the commission tasked with determining the causes of the fall of Western Slavonia; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: As a member of that commission, together with other members, when you were adopting the conclusions that have been discussed here, did you have in your hands a directive from 1994, the document that I showed to you yesterday, if you remember, the directive to carry out Operation Flash in December 1994? Did you have at your disposal that document when you were making your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the light of that document, now that you have seen it, now that you saw it two days ago, what do you think about the conclusions made by that commission in which you participated? Would the conclusions made by that commission have been the same had you had that document at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would have changed a lot of things, but we, in our commission reviewed primarily our own problems and responsibilities at our level, without going further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your answer - and I stand to be corrected - you mean that the conclusions of your commission would have been different if you had had this document at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And to conclude, during yesterday's cross-examination, the Prosecutor put to you the position of the international community. He said that the international community, without specifying what exactly he means, accepted the use of force in Western Slavonia. You told us two days ago, in response to one of my questions, that on two occasions in 2001 you provided statements to OTP investigators about events in Western Slavonia about Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On those two occasions, did the investigators of the ICTY inform you of this position of the international community? Did they inform you that all your work was an exercise in futility in view of such a position of the international community?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. If I may go back to that question that I said must be expunged, not only the question but also the answer to it, that is page 3, lines 15 to 17, must be completely expunged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, I have one little question, which would be a clarification concerning a document which we saw. Can we have the document again on the screen. It was 925, Exhibit 9 -- Court Exhibit 925. Yes, thank you. It's on the screen. Here we have this letter of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence of 30 August 1991 to, it says in English, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Greguric. And in the original version, in B/C/S version - and this is what you read out and then it was translated to us literally - it was addressed to "Gospodine Predsednice". Do you see that? And you translated these words. How did you translate that or how did you read -- how did the translator interpret it? It was interpreted as a president. "Predsednice," this is president, isn't it? So was he the president or the prime minister? Who was Mr. Franjo Greguric at that time, in late August 1991? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the B/C/S we use the term that would literally be translated as president of government and rarely do we address that person as premier or prime minister. That would be the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that means he was the chancellor, the prime minister, as it is usually said in other countries? The prime minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was my only question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just have one area also. Could you please tell me, at the date of establishment of the SAOK, which territories or republics were within the Yugoslav union?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Republic of Slovenia was still there, the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Macedonia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did this situation continue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My apologies. Thank you. Did this situation continue until the establishment of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slovenia seceded at that point in time, whereas Croatia had not, not as yet, not at the time of the establishment of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, at the time of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: At the time of 1993 and 1994, which countries were left in the union? Or which republics, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there remained Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and the two provinces within Serbia, Vojvodina and Kosovo. Macedonia, Slovenia and Croatia had made the decision on secession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So the JNA would essentially have been an army for those constituent territories as a union.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would there -- let me think about what I'm going to ask. In terms of that fact, would there have arisen any conflict in the joinder of any particular territory with the JNA in terms of conflict with another territory within the union?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find the question a bit confusing. Do you mean the three republics that were left - Serbia, Bosnia and Montenegro? Did you mean to say that there would have occurred a conflict among these three republics without Slovenia, Croatia and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take that as a given.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat. I find the question, again, a bit puzzling. I'm not sure whether you are referring to the three republics, namely Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia, whether there, there would have been a conflict with the JNA. That is my understanding of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Do you see, in your mind, any conflict with, say, Serbia joining the RSK in a conflict with Croatia, having regard to the constituent republics of the union that was now left that constituted Yugoslavia? Or to put it differently --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to speculate about things that may or may not occur. I can only give you my thoughts about this probable conflict, because the JNA still existed as an armed force in organisational terms. And it is quite certain that any unit that came under attack would defend itself, any JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I probably have not helped you, but were there not joint efforts between the JNA units and units of the RSK, armed forces of the RSK? Joint military operations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, with the retreating of the JNA units, which was completed by the 30th of June, 1992, except for a handful of officers who belonged to the army, there were no other JNA units in that area. The only ones who stayed behind were officers who hailed from the area, but that was just a handful of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, yesterday when you were asked questions by the Prosecutor, you said the following: That you joined the SAO Krajina TO on the 1st of April of 1992. Do you remember that? You also said to him that you joined the SVK in December 1992 and you were a member of the SVK until 1995. Do you remember that? You further went on to say, while you were a member of this TO and SVK you remained a member of the JNA and received pay from the JNA, and then subsequently the VJ. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: Were there other soldiers of the JNA who joined the south Krajina TO, like you, and also perhaps joined the SVK like you, but remained members of the JNA and continued to receive salaries from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, regular JNA soldiers, and I mean conscripts who were serving their obligatory military service in Krajina, there were none of them. There were just some commissioned and non-commissioned officers who were native of the area and who asked of their own will to be seconded to the Krajina army from the JNA. I was among the group, simply because I felt the need to be with my people, as a professional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Would you like to come closer to my question? Just tell me if there were other people, other soldiers in your position who joined SAO Krajina TO and the SVK but remained members of the JNA and continued to receive a salary from the JNA, and subsequently from the VJ. You should be able to say, "Yes, there were such people," "No, there were no such people," or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just a handful of them, really, who were not natives of Krajina and who were volunteers and joined us over there. I don't think they were as many as ten even. And they were not from Krajina but nevertheless asked to be there. They would serve in Krajina for six months, whereupon they would return back to their units in Serbia or elsewhere. So they stayed there only for a limited period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with this few. While they were in the Krajina for that period of six months, they were paid by the JNA. That's a question: Were they paid by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, those are the people who were not natives of SAO Krajina. What about the natives of SAO Krajina, who were in your position? Were there any who joined the SAO Krajina TO and later joined the SVK but remained JNA members and continued to receive a salary from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of them received their salaries from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While they were members of the SAO Krajina TO, and also while they were members of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to find out from you. Any questions arising from the Chamber? Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hope just one or two questions about dates arising from Her Honour Judge Nosworthy's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric just one or two things that shouldn't take long. Is it correct that Croatia declared its independence on the 25th of June, 1991? Is that the date that Croatia -- or that's the date that Croatia declared independence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I know that there was a declaration. But whether it was a declaration on independence or not, I believe that such declaration was only adopted in November or December of 1991. I doubt that it occurred on the 25th of June, although I cannot speak about it with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So am I to understand that you don't really know whether or not Croatia declared independence in June of 1991. You think it was later, but you can't really remember; is that fair? If not, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Slovenia declared its independence at that point, but I'm not sure about Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know -- did you know that on the 8th of October, 1991 Croatia broke off its relations with the SFRY? Do you know about that occurring on the 8th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truly, I don't know the dates. I do know that Croatia broke off its relations as soon as the HDZ came to power. But I don't know the dates, I can't tell you that, no. This was the reality of politics and I didn't take much interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's quite all right if you don't know the dates. It's quite all right if you say so. That's fine. Do you remember, probably, though that on the 19th of December, 1991, that is when the RSK was proclaimed; right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Peric, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to testify in this case. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told that a question was raised by the Defence about the reason behind the adjournment on the 6th -- I beg your pardon, the 2nd to the 6th of October that is mentioned in a decision that was handed down yesterday. Is that correct, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time we raised that issue, we did not have the full decision in our hands. We could anticipate at what this recess was directed. We just wanted to know whether this had to do with the earlier plans of the Trial Chamber or not. We are in public session and I would not wish to state, in public, the main reason behind raising this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, yes, we were made aware of the possible expectation that there may have been a change on those plans. There are no changes on those plans. Those plans still stand as they are. Let me just give the reason for that break. It has just come to this Trial Chamber's attention that in between recesses Chambers are allowed a week off just to recharge batteries, and we thought we could take that week at that time. What influenced the decision to place it at that time is that Judge Nosworthy, who sits in this Trial Chamber and in the Milutinovic Trial Chamber, will be having a break in that week in the Milutinovic trial. And if we took it at any other time, it means she would never rest, she would never recharge. Her batteries would just go flat -- she says they have gone flat right now. So we thought we must synchronise it with Milutinovic so she also gets an opportunity to recharge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am grateful for this explanation. It was not out of mere curiosity that we raised this matter. We simply wanted to check whether that obligation we had on the 25th had been put back, or not. That was what we wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. It's just as I say, as I have explained, okay? Thank you very much. Next witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence calls the next Defence witness, and that is Mr. Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like we are digging him from deep, this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since he is under no protective measures, I hope he will be easy to find. We are waiting, and will accept any decision you choose to make. Maybe we can take a break early, if you see that fitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently he is being brought, but he had been apparently scheduled for quarter to four, so he's now being dug out from a little deeper than five past three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems -- it seemed realistic that he could start from week two, and we have been too efficient maybe. Maybe that's the reason for his delay. Otherwise, we were ready to continue today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he is here? Is he here? Fine. That's fine. Let's wait for him. It does seem as if we are really digging deep. Maybe let's take a break. I'm not quite sure how we shall be advised when to reconvene, because it's anybody's guess when he will arrive. May I suggest that as we stretch our legs, we stay around our offices so that when we get advised, we can come back quickly. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delay. It's one of those matters. I'm sorry about that. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence team, I, as Defence counsel for Mr. Martic, will be leading your examination-in-chief. Before we begin, can I please ask you to make a brief pause between questions and answers so that the interpreters can follow. It is our mutual obligation. Could you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Popovic. I am from Sibenik. I was born on the 1st of January, 1939, in Bogotic, Drnis municipality, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's saved me a few questions. Could you tell us your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your religion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were born somewhere in Drnis municipality. Can you tell us where you finished primary and secondary school, and if you have a university degree.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The first three years of primary school I completed in my native Bogatic, and I continued schooling in Belgrade, where I lived with my uncle. I finished the fourth year of primary school there and four years of high school. In 1954, I returned to Knin where I continued my schooling in high school in Knin, secondary school in Knin. After that, in 1958, I went to Belgrade again to enrol in the law school of the Belgrade University. I graduated in 1963, in November 1963 in the stream called "Justice System".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you found your first job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: My first job was in Sibenik, to which I returned from Belgrade, and that was on the 1st of February, 1966. I found a job in the factory of electrodes and ferro alloys, but after two months, I transferred to the Jadranska Banka in Sibenik. I was a legal assistant in my trial period, after which I became a legal clerk and later became head of the legal service that I helped set up myself, because at the outset I was the only one who had a law degree in that bank that was in the process of being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me until when you worked in Jadranska Banka in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 31st of March, 1991. I worked there for over 20 years. But I didn't leave of my own will, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness spent his entire career in Sibenik, I would like to refer you to pages 30/31 of our atlas. Sibenik is in quadrant B2. It's a place south-west of Knin and Drnis, approximately midway between Zadar and Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So until the end of March, 1991, you were a lawyer in this bank, Jadranska Banka. Did you live in Sibenik all that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got married there as well and had two daughters; Nadasa in 1968 and Branka in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an apartment there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived there, or maybe a year later, I received an apartment. It was allocated to me as a highly qualified and valued staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your employment, were you involved in any social activities in that period from 1966 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: For several years I was not involved in any political or social work and I was not a member of the ruling party. However, from 1971 onwards, I got involved in the setting up of a cultural society called Prosvjeta, a Serb cultural society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. Can you tell us: Did you establish that society, and how long did it exist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: We established it, I believe it was on the 16th of June, 1971, in Sibenik. I was a member of the main board of that society, which was based in Zagreb, and throughout Croatia in various towns, branches of the society were set up. This cultural society was a centralized one with branches all over the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the line of work, the purpose of that society?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the society was to spread and preserve the culture and traditions of the Serbian people in Croatia, and for Serbs, who, until then, had no cultural institutions in Croatia, because all societies and their property had been destroyed in the Second World War, and whatever remained was later nationalised by the state, such as the buildings of Serbian schools, publishing houses, print works, and other property that Serbs used to have in the times of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. It is necessary to stress that this society was created at the time of the so-called maspok in Croatia, mass movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You still haven't answered my question. What was the purpose of that society? Or maybe you think you did answer the question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I could add that one of the purposes of the society was to foster the tradition of the Serbian people and developing cultural activities, preserving the Cyrillic script in Croatia that had been suppressed and practically did not exist anymore, and to struggle for the promotion of cultural institutions, Serbian cultural institutions in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did this society exist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Not very long at all, because the state authorities and the party authorities which prevailed in the then Republic of Croatia, in the course of fighting against the mass movement and the socialist system that prevailed then, banned the work of the main society, called Matica Srpska, and also our work in order to establish a sort of symmetry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. The question, sir, had been: How long did this society of yours exist for? Can you give us a year or a month or a date where it disbanded, if it did disband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it practically ceased to work after just six months after the debate and the very process of getting established. And it was abolished by a decree of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia because it had allegedly stopped working. That happened a bit later. I can't tell you exactly when this decree was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will stop you at this time. Was this in 1971 or later?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It was somewhat later. As we discontinued our activities, we were no longer able to have any bearing on the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you think it necessary to put any additional questions on this matter? I believe the witness answered your question, but maybe you have some other queries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, what I don't understand is this last question where he says: "No. It was somewhat later." I thought he had said it existed for six months. Now, if it was established, as he said, earlier in June of 1971, then by December 1971 it should have stopped existing. I'm not quite sure what happened. "It was somewhat later." What happened? I don't know whether the decree of the Ministry of the Interior came somewhat later, because he says the reason for the decree was that the society was not operative any longer. So it's all confusing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for this suggestion and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that you set up the Serbian cultural society called Prosvjeta. You stated that the society existed for several months. What were its activities in this period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one needs to know that the society was set up at the time when this populace mass movement gained momentum in Croatia, which was separatist in character and which set in motion the procedure for the review of the federal constitution and the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, with a view to allowing Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia. This was at the time of the constitutional reform, and Croatian nationalists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. May I ask you, Witness - we don't have much time - may I ask you to please listen very carefully to the question that is asked and try to answer the question as briefly and as succinctly as you possibly can. The question to you is: What were its activities in this period? You are telling us what prevailed at the time this movement was in existence. Listen to the question. Tell us the activities of your movement at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the very outset, right after the establishment of the society, we organised several seminars on the Serb language, where eminent linguists of the Serb language held their lectures. They came from Belgrade. We also organised several poetry events involving poets from Serbia who were supposed to come to Dalmatia and hold several literary evenings. Thus we organised a visit by an author from Serbia, and a literary evening was supposed to be held in the town of Zadar. However, the Zadar authorities did not permit this evening to go ahead. It was supposed to take place in a cultural hall. That was why we took the poet to the area of Benkovac, near Zadar. That was at the place call Islam Grcki. And we had a poetry evening that was held outdoors. Over 15.000 people attended the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this was a cultural event of sorts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other such activities? You said that you ceased to be active six months later. Why? I also have to draw your attention to the following matter: The interpretation service is doing their job very well and you're speaking pace is fine. You are not excessively speeding; that is why you can talk as you normally do.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is noteworthy that our activities were carried out under the close supervision and surveillance on the part of the police. Our activists were continually harassed; some of them were even brought in to the police stations for the so-called interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Did such an attitude and treatment of your activists lead to the discontinuance of your activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it then that the SUP, the Ministry of the Interior, passed a decree to the effect that because the society had ceased to be active, it was to be closed down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the aftermath of the year 1971, during which you were active in this society called Prosvjeta, did you continue engaging in social activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1989 I was no longer engaged in any political or other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you had been working as a lawyer in a bank for 25 years, that you were the head of the legal service, and that between 1971 and 1989 you no longer engaged in any social activities. You only had your career to tend to. What happened in 1989?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. He said political or other activities, at least that was the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. I had this in mind. I did not wish to misrepresent his testimony. I merely wanted to speed up the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please, you have to caution me if at any moment I misstate your statement. Therefore, after the activities you were engaged in 1971, what were the activities you became involved in in 1989?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1989, the event commemorating 600 years of the Kosovo battle was organised in Croatia under the auspices of the Croatian parliament. Serb intellectuals from Dalmatia launched an initiative for the establishment of the Serb cultural society called Zora, based in Knin, in this period of time. Alongside the anniversary event, they also held their founding Assembly in Kistanje, near to the Krka monastery, where the festivities concerning the 600th anniversary were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, alongside this anniversary, there was an attempt to establish the Serb cultural society Zora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in fact established, and what happened next? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The police dispersed this gathering, and after a certain period of time, they arrested all the persons involved in the founding of this society and among them was the president of the society, Jovan Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I am doing so in order to take you through the examination. Were there any proceedings instituted against Jovan Opacic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings were instituted against Jovan Opacic in Sibenik. I believe that he was arrested in November in his home town of Plavno and taken to the prison in Sibenik. Over 25 lawyers from throughout Yugoslavia were involved in his defence, because this case had a very high profile throughout Yugoslavia. He was acquitted because he had apparently committed only the crime of speech. Apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1989, did there come any political changes in the territory of the then Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: There ensued wide-ranging and radical changes in that tendencies appeared toward a multi-party system. This led to an explosion of nationalist sentiment in Croatia, because the Croatian nationalist forces realised that the time had come to again become engaged in an attempt that failed back in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the gist of the attempt, what the attempt was about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The main purpose was to bring about a secession of Croatia from Yugoslavia and to set up an independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time did you become involved politically, and with whom, if so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became part of the founding committee of the Serbian Democratic Party. As a long-time friend of a medical doctor from Sibenik, Jovan Raskovic, and several other intellectuals from Dalmatia, I joined them in launching the initiative for the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we turn to the establishment of the SDS, I will ask you something about Mr. Jovan Raskovic. Who is he? You said that he is a friend of yours. You've known him for many years. Who was that man?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after my arrival in Sibenik, I got to know Mr. Jovan Raskovic because he also hailed from my home area, the Krajina. He was an eminent physician and an intellectual par excellence. He took part in many symposiums on psychiatry and organised them, like the one renowned symposium held in Opatija, which was at an international level. And he took part in many medical congresses around the world. That is why one can say that he is of the rank of intellectuals such as Habermas, Eric Fromme and Sartre. He, in fact, had correspondence with many renowned intellectuals in Europe, so that, for instance, at one point when the police searched his premises, they came across the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that later.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that he was well respected and popular, loved by the people. He was a great personality, because he was very close to everyone. And there wasn't a single family in Sibenik and in its environs that did not use his services as a psychiatrist, neurologist. He even studied and was a renowned anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe your relations and friendship?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after my arrival in Sibenik, through my wife, who is a native Sibenik and is a teacher of languages, of the English language, I got to know this circle of intellectuals among whom was Jovan Raskovic. It was thus that through my wife and her friends I got to know him. Throughout my stay in Sibenik, I was on very close terms with him. Our families socialized.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described Jovan Raskovic as a European intellectual. Can resentment, hatred or intolerance be in any way tied up with his personality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was a soft-spoken person, a great humanitarian who got involved in politics precisely because he witnessed the suffering and hardships of the people who had been persecuted ever since 1971 by this fascist regime, and this regime continued its aggression in 1991. So that many people sought protection by asking to be admitted into the psychiatric ward. This was a way of avoiding persecutions, particularly at workplaces where this practice was widespread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that later. Can you tell us until what point did you socialize with Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I socialized with him until his death on the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago in one of your answers that Croatia saw the emergence of political pluralism and the establishment of several political parties, and you, with your friends and Dr. Jovan Raskovic, started thinking about establishing the Serbian Democratic Party. Can you tell us at what time was that in 1989?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The initiative to establish that party started precisely at the time of that commemoration I mentioned and the incidents I referred to a moment ago. And one date I can remember is the 9th of November, 1989, which is when Bogoljub Popovic came to see me in Sibenik. He was a retired JNA colonel. And he wanted to talk to me about what name to give to the party we thought we would establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt you. You said: "Bogoljub Popovic came to see me." Were you alone at the time? And how come you remember the date? It was a long time ago, 1989.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the date because just after that 9th of November, only two days later, eight agents of the Croatian secret police barged into the apartment of Dr. Jovan Raskovic in Sibenik with a search warrant, because he was under suspicion of being a leader of a terrorist Chetnik organisation, which was totally preposterous of course. They spent the whole day searching his apartment as well as his weekend cottage in Primosten. And since it was my habit to take a walk every evening, there in the field in Primosten, I was surprised not to see him there. I saw him late at night, when he was completely exhausted after the day he had. He told me about the search, about how the police found letters he had received from Dr. Fromme and Dr. Habermas. And then the same thing happened to this colonel, Bogoljub Popovic who had been to see us. And he was mistreated for about 16 hours until he asked for a lawyer, and then they released him. Of course, no charges were brought because there was no grounds for any charges, nor was there any evidence that they were involved in any Chetnik organisation or terrorist organisation. But it was the favorite expression among certain Croatian circles to use that term, "Chetnik," when referring to Serbs. And even today, you can hear the same rhetoric at some Croatian meetings to denote all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you remember that day in November because of that dramatic event, the search of the apartment of Dr. Raskovic and the arrest and search of the apartment of the other friend you told us about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Despite this action of the secret police, did you continue your activities? And how did it all end? Can you tell us, briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view that was just an attempt to intimidate Dr. Jovan Raskovic, to make him give up the idea to establish the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia. And if they had managed to do that, half of the job of the Croatian authorities would have been done. They would have had an easy time of dealing with the others. However, Dr. Raskovic decided to go to the bitter end in this struggle, because it was about not only his life but the life of his entire people, and there was no way he would withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just said Dr. Raskovic said -- Dr. Raskovic was prepared to go to the bitter end in this showdown. What did you mean by that? What did Dr. Raskovic continue to do until the end?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: We convened a meeting of this founding committee. We drafted a statute of the Serb Democratic Party and decided that it would be the Autochthonous Party of the Serbian People in Croatia, and that we would get involved in the debate about the constitutional position of the Serb people in Croatia that had just started and that didn't bode well for the Serbian people at all. And on the 17th of February, 1990, we organised our founding assembly in Knin, at the railway station, or rather the square outside the railway station in Knin. Let me just note that we held all our larger rallies in the open because we had no resources to provide the necessary security in any of the larger cities in Croatia, especially not in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this founding assembly of the SDS held?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of February, 1990, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you just said that it was held in Knin, near the railway station, Sibenik was much larger town than Knin. Why didn't you hold it in Sibenik or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Some people proposed that as well, but it was practically impossible to organise, because we couldn't find enough people who would agree to become members of those founding committees, because people were so afraid that they would lose their jobs, that their families would be exposed to all sorts of unpleasantries and harassment. There was, you could say, a paranoid fear that prevailed. And of course we didn't like it, but we had to understand and accept it, because people are people. They're afraid for their own skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that founding assembly in Knin on the 17th of February, did you elect some bodies of the party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Board, consisting of 21 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the president and secretary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The president was Jovan Raskovic and the secretary or, rather, the General Secretary, as we called it, was myself, Branko Popovic. I chaired that founding assembly, as a member of the working presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was required by the legislation at that time for a party to exist and to operate normally? And did you fulfil those requirements?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: A party had to have a certain number of members in the founding committee, to have held the founding assembly, and to have elected the main bodies, such as the Main Board, president and secretary. And the party had to register with the Ministry of Justice and Administration in Zagreb. I did all that, as the secretary. I did all the paperwork and had the party registered in Zagreb. And then we started -- we proceeded to establish further committees and boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see now on the screen document 138. It's the entry of the SDS party in the register of political parties of Croatia. Let me just show it to you, Witness, and you will tell me if you recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see -- or rather enlarge the heading, the left top corner, please. Can we see that and maybe zoom in.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "Republic Secretariat".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what is this decision about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision to enter the Serb Democratic Party in the register of political organizations. That means that the party was legal and registered and that it was entitled to proceed and establish its boards at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any longer. You say after the establishment of the Main Board on the 17th of February, 1990 at Knin, the party was registered, and after that you proceeded to organise local boards of the party. In which areas, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: We proceeded to organise them everywhere in Croatia, where there was enough interest in our party. We went to Dalmatia first, Lika, Kordun, Banija. All of these are districts of Croatia. Then we moved to Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you here, Mr. Popovic. The party was established on the 17th of February, 1990, and registered in March 1990. When were the first multi-party elections in Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: In April, that was the first round of elections, and the second round was in May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who won? And how many votes did the Serb Democratic Party win?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The elections were won by Tudjman's Croatian Democratic Union, whereas the Serb Democratic Party from Knin won five seats in the Croatian parliament, whereas at the local level it won a majority in Knin, Gracac, Donja Lapac, Obrovac, Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, when I interrupt you, don't continue. I will come back to any question to which I did not get a sufficient answer. Can we say, therefore, that the Serb Democratic Party won a majority in just a few municipalities in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was six municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. Can you tell us, if you have that information, who did the majority of the Serb population vote for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They voted in the majority for the SDP and the League of Communists of Croatia. SDP was a party led by Racan. I think they had 33 seats in the parliament, their party, and we had five seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction, if any, of the Croatian authorities and Croatian media to the organising of the Serb Democratic Party and its work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was a reaction. There was a vicious campaign against us. Croatian media were busy creating a Serbo-phobic atmosphere to discredit us, to intimidate people. There were even cases when Croatian television used a montage to show that there was drunken group at each one of our rallies on which they would zoom in. I don't know where they found them, but they zoomed in on every rally on a group wearing Serb caps, seemingly drunk, that looked like Chetniks, although those were areas that were traditionally partizan in the Second World War. And I don't know, actually, how they found them, but they always zoomed in on some alleged Chetnik groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say the Croatian press and television detected some Chetnik groups. Where? What are you talking about exactly? In what places?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at our assemblies, because they were large gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which assemblies exactly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: At our rallies they were all public and they were all registered, and the turnout was huge. I don't know where they found those drunken groups to paint this picture in the Croatian public eye about our party. But it was not the only thing. All our activists who took part in those assemblies were stigmatised and demonised wherever they lived. And they would take stills from those assemblies and print photos and put them up on the doors of various workplaces where these people worked. So there was obviously a public campaign against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question of the witness. You mentioned seemingly drunk persons that looked like Chetniks. What does a Chetnik look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have these very characteristic caps with specific insignia which contain the coat of arms normally worn by the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Some people wore these caps and this was not a prohibited conduct. We had our stewards who took care of order at these rallies. After all, the freedom of movement and assembly was proclaimed after the multi-party elections, and people started wearing uniforms and specific dress worn by the armies back in history, and so on and so forth. This did not constitute prohibited behaviour. However, the mass media in Croatia, the television, used the stills in order to represent our party as primitive. There was this one person who tried to prevent these incidents from happening and he tried to control the damage. But I do remember that there were provocations at each and every one of our rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Do you have any other questions on this topic or can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Two questions. Is he saying that the Chetniks wore uniforms? And I am also observing that I had believed that the word "Chetnik" or a term was pejorative or derogatory, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that's true. It was used pejoratively, because they would not have a full uniform. They would wear a cap. But at any rate, they were not members of any military formations. There were no such formations in 1990. There weren't any armed formations, and there was still relative peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you spoke of assemblies or gatherings of the Serb Democratic Party in various places, which were, as you say, attended by large groups of people. And then the Croatian television would only zoom in on some individuals who looked like Chetniks who wore these caps with cockades and were seemingly drunk. What did you mean to say about this? What was the purpose of all of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to present all of us leaders of the SDS and the party itself in an unfavourable light, to demonise us and make it impossible for us to be active locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that ordinary citizens who would come to attend these meetings of your party were exposed to unpleasantries because they would be filmed or shot there, and then their pictures would show up at their workplace. What did this mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: That meant that their work associates who were members of other Croatian parties, notably the HDZ, knew who these persons were and applied certain measures against them; for instance, lock them out of their workplaces; ban them from entering the premises. For instance, the manager of my bank told me after these activities in which I was involved, a group of people came to the bank on behalf of the Croatian authorities and said that I should be dismissed from work. And I said that I could not accept this, but the manager told me, "Well, you still have 15 days of annual leave. You should take a holiday, at least for a while. Lie low until the matter is settled." But the things were not going to settle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that your party was registered in February, your bodies were established in March, and the elections were in May, all of it in 1990. These media coverages of your party, showing you in an unfavourable light, when did they take place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after we started holding these rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Popovic, did this have any bearing on interethnic relations in Sibenik and the general area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Of course they did. I witnessed them myself. I saw what effects this propaganda had on people's characters and sentiments. I was a person who people knew, and I held a high position in the bank where I was able to intercede on behalf of many people. I will give you one illustration of what I have in mind, just to show you what sort of things can happen when people are involved. Every day I would go and buy newspapers at this one kiosk at a neighbourhood of Sibenik called Sibenska Poljana. On this particular day we were involved in the activities around the founding of the party. In addition to other newspapers, I normally bought Politika, which was a daily from Belgrade. The lady selling the papers, who I had known for years and whom I had taken to see Mr. Raskovic because she had pains in the neck, she told me, "Mr. Popovic, would you be so kind as to take me to Professor Raskovic, as I am suffering from terrible headaches?" And I told her, "Well, when I will have one of our walks in the evening, I will see what I can do about it." And, in fact, I managed to organise an appointment with Mr. Raskovic. And she told me that she would never forget this favour of mine, because she did not even have to wait for a long time. She was able to see Dr. Raskovic for a neurological checkup. She was delighted with that. However, several days later, as I came to buy newspapers at her kiosk, she told me, "I'm sorry, I can no longer sell any newspapers to you." And I said, "Why?" She said, "My dignity and pride will not allow me to do that." I was shocked. I didn't know what this was about. This was a place where I had been buying newspapers for 25 years. I saw a group of militant HDZ members who were across from the kiosk in front of a cafe, and I realised that it was them, that they had lead her to act this way. I did not really expect her to listen to them, especially in view of the fact that I had helped her. I did not expect any special gratitude, but nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you experienced any unpleasantries at your workplace.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I had such unpleasant experiences back in 1971, but of course at that point there was the Karadjordjevo meeting where these things were put to a stop. Tito intervened. However, at this point in 1990, there was no one to put a stop to that. It was in that context that my manager called me to see him and told me that these people had come and asked that I be disallowed from entering the premises of the bank. He tried to persuade me to take my annual leave, to be absent for a fortnight, in the hope that things would settle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What position did you hold at the time when you had this conversation with your manager, and what position did you hold later on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: At that point I was the head of the legal department, and then I took my annual leave. But this was the reason why I took my annual leave, because an initiative was launched in Sibenik involving a petition that was supposed to be signed and which said that Jovan Raskovic, Dobrijevic and I should be expelled from Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a petition was circulated which was supposed to be signed involving the expulsion of yourself and others. When was this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 30th of August, 1990, when, at the central square in Sibenik, outside the theatre where banners were placed, there was a desk with banners containing the text of the petition. The contents of the petition were really quite unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it stated, briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It said that Raskovic, Dobrijevic and I had no place among them, and that they would be more than happy to see us away from this particular community, because we, in no way, deserved to be among them. The signing of the petition was something that covered two days and over 20.000 citizens signed the petition. These books were delivered to the Sibenik mayor. This meant that as of that day, we were persona non grata in the town of Sibenik and that everyone was free to persecute us wherever we were in the area, without any sanctions whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Popovic, you spoke about the signing of the petition in the town of Sibenik aimed at expelling the three leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party. Do you know who was the leader of that petition, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person who organised that petition to drive us out from the town was the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, and some other Croatian parties were involved. But it was mainly the Croatian Democratic Union. They first organised the expulsion of Mr. Raskovic from Sibenik, where he had a vacation home, although he had spent a lot of time in Sibenik and treated many people in that town. He was well loved and respected. Nevertheless, he became a persona non grata over night and had to leave that vacation home that was later bombed. His entire library, consisting of over 2.000 medical books, perished. After that petition, his colleagues intercepted him outside the hospital where he went every morning and told him: "You are not welcome here because you are working against the Croatian state." He just turned around and never came back. I think it was after the 28th of August, 1990 that he submitted his resignation, because it made no sense for him to go there any more. His colleagues in the Sibenik hospital watched him pursively as the militants of the HDZ prevented Raskovic from entering the hospital without lifting a finger, and that hurt him a lot more than what the young militants did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you here. Was this petition reported in the media?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, they did, with great relish. All the mass media in Croatia wrote about that monstrous petition as something good, something that would disable Raskovic from going on with his work. But they forgot about the impression it would create in the international community; they completely lost sight of that. The atmosphere was delirical. The HDZ wrote about that petition widely, inviting other citizens from other towns to join in, so that people even came from other towns to Sibenik to increase the number of signatures on the petition. I also learned later that in Split, which is about 80 kilometres away from Sibenik, the signing of the same petition was organised in a fish shop. A relative of mine told me that, a relative who lived on the island of Hvar and saw this petition with my name on it in Split. This proves that Croatian authorities knew about it and they organised it themselves. I forgot to say that this was already after the victory of the HDZ at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was after -- rather, in late August 1990, and you told us it was your impression that the organizers lost sight of the impression it would make outside. But what was the effect on the rest of the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: From that moment on, it was impossible for us to go on living in that town. I was unable to leave my apartment without being intercepted by those militants of the HDZ. They would immediately start shouting, calling us names, calling us Chetniks. Jovan Raskovic was unable to leave his apartment, and he even begged me to bring him mineral water because he didn't dare step outside. We waited for the young men, who usually drove us to founding assemblies when we were supposed to go to other towns, to take us somewhere. And when those young men came to pick him up, he would just run quickly into the car before the militants rushed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And would they really rush in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of that atmosphere of aggression, he insisted on taking our daily walk. And I was an eyewitness when those young men moved in on him to strike him. And he was a weak man after an accident that he had, and they were about to hit him when I stopped them, trying to protect him. But I couldn't always protect him and I suggested it wasn't safe to go out anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say those young men moved in to strike him. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They were young militants, members of the HDZ. They would throw some incendiary, what do you call them, cocktails on our homes, slash our car tyres. We couldn't go anywhere. Whenever we would try to go somewhere by car, we would find all four tyres slashed. Whenever we went to any enterprise, nobody wanted to talk to us. After that petition, when I went to my former bank, the receptionist simply ran away from me when I said hello. Everybody kept their heads down and nobody dared greet me. I just sat there, doing nothing. My license was taken away from me, because until then I had been the legal representative of the bank and now I couldn't appear in court anymore. And I just sat there listening to their favorite music that they played deliberately from those boomboxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Can we now look at Exhibit 880. It's a copy of one page from the Zagreb daily Vjesnik. The issue is dated the 25th of August, 1990. We are interested in page 2. This is the story in a Zagreb daily about an interim session of the parliament of Croatia, an extraordinary session. And it says that a meeting was held, a session of the Croatian parliament was held to discuss the political situation and the unrest in some municipalities. We see this article in front of us now. Can we please zoom in on the third column from the left. The middle column, yes. I will read to you one part of the text, Mr. Popovic. "A member of parliament, Ratko Licina, spoke there and, among other things, he said: This, that is continuing to happen to the Serbian people in Sibenik and Primosten, where for two days now signatures are being collected to have Jovan Raskovic, Branko Popovic and Marko Dobrijevic expelled is a fascist persecution orchestrated by the democratically elected Croatian leadership. Croatian mass media are being run in an unprecedented way by the authorities and are writing with great relish about this event." We can see that the parliament was familiar with these events. Did they do anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Croatian authorities did not do a thing to protect us from this tyranny, this spreading aggression of the Croatian public. This tyranny can turn your every day life into hell. It doesn't kill you, but it makes every day life impossible. And you don't know what to do. Out of sheer spite, I stayed on for another eight months after the petition, but I could see that I couldn't stand it for much longer, because nobody is talking to you, nobody acknowledges you, and you live surrounded by silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Do you know, perhaps, if any other residents of Croatia who were Serbs experienced the same problems at the time, the same aggression?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you could say that there are three types, three levels of that aggression. One was the instrumental aggression by the Croatian parliament, because not a single of our Serb demands could pass in that Croato-centric parliament, and on lower levels the same thing was going on, starting with the police and spreading everywhere else. So that's the instrumental aggression of the Croatian parliament. Then there was systemic aggression. First of all, we were thrown out of the Croatian constitution. Then there was systemic aggression at the level of authorities. And at the local level was what I call dispersive aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
